lists.title: French A1 Grammar Path
lists.description: A1 grammar in communicative order: subject pronouns, noun gender and number, both article families, être and avoir, the three verb groups in the present, negation, il y a, questions, and adjective agreement.

points.title: Subject pronouns (je, tu, il…)
points.function: Say who you are talking about
points.explanation:
The subject pronouns are je (I), tu (you, informal), il/elle (he/she), on (one/we, informal), nous (we), vous (you, formal or plural), ils/elles (they). Vous doubles as the polite singular — use it with strangers.

On is how spoken French usually says 'we': on mange à midi.
points.culture_note: Choosing tu or vous is a real social decision. When unsure, start with vous and wait to be invited to tutoyer.

references.title: Vitrine linguistique (BDL) — Office québécois de la langue française

points.title: Gender and number of nouns
points.function: Name people and things, one or many
points.explanation:
Every noun is masculine or feminine — learn each noun with its gender, because little about the word itself tells you.

The plural usually adds a silent -s (livre → livres); since it isn't pronounced, the article carries the plural out loud.

Endings give clues: -tion and -té are usually feminine, -age and -eau usually masculine.

points.title: Definite articles (le / la / les)
points.function: Point to a specific thing
points.explanation:
Le before masculine nouns (le livre), la before feminine (la maison), les for any plural (les livres). Before a vowel or silent h, le and la both shrink to l' (l'école).

French uses the definite article far more than English — also for general statements: j'aime le café (I like coffee).

points.title: Indefinite articles (un / une / des)
points.function: Mention something for the first time
points.explanation: Un before masculine nouns (un chien), une before feminine (une maison), and — unlike English — a plural indefinite des (des amis, 'some friends'). Des is required where English just drops the article: j'ai des questions.

points.title: Être — present (je suis, tu es…)
points.function: Say who or what someone is
points.explanation:
Être (to be) is wildly irregular and everywhere: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont.

Professions take no article after être: elle est professeur.

points.title: Avoir — present (j'ai faim)
points.function: Say what you have — and how you feel
points.explanation:
Avoir (to have): j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont.

French uses avoir where English uses 'to be' for states: avoir faim (be hungry), avoir soif (be thirsty), avoir vingt ans (be twenty), avoir raison (be right).
points.culture_note: Never say 'je suis vingt ans' — age is something you HAVE in French.

points.title: Present tense of -er verbs
points.function: Talk about what people do
points.explanation:
Ninety percent of French verbs end in -er and share one pattern.

Drop -er, add: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent (parler → je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent).

Four of those six forms sound identical — the pronoun does the work in speech.

points.title: -ir and -re verbs (finir, vendre)
points.function: Finish, choose, wait, sell — the other two families
points.explanation:
-ir verbs like finir: je finis, tu finis, il finit, nous finissons (note the -iss- in the plural), vous finissez, ils finissent.

-re verbs like vendre: je vends, tu vends, il vend, nous vendons, vous vendez, ils vendent.

Attendre (wait), entendre (hear), and choisir (choose) follow these patterns.

points.title: Negation with ne … pas
points.function: Say what is not so
points.explanation:
Negation wraps the verb in a frame: ne + verb + pas. Je ne parle pas anglais.

Before a vowel, ne becomes n': je n'aime pas. After a negation, un/une/des become de: je n'ai pas de chien.
points.culture_note: In casual speech the ne often disappears — je parle pas. Learn the full frame first; drop it later like the locals.

points.title: Il y a — there is / there are
points.function: Say what exists or is available
points.explanation:
Il y a covers both 'there is' and 'there are' — it never changes for plural: il y a un livre, il y a deux livres. Negative: il n'y a pas de… (no article, just de).

Question: est-ce qu'il y a… ?

points.title: Question words (où, comment, quand…)
points.function: Ask about places, people, time, and reasons
points.explanation:
Où (where), comment (how), quand (when), que/qu' (what), pourquoi (why), combien (how much/many), qui (who).

Three ways to build a question: intonation (tu viens ?), est-ce que (est-ce que tu viens ?), or inversion (viens-tu ?) — est-ce que is the everyday workhorse.

points.title: Adjective agreement
points.function: Describe people and things correctly
points.explanation:
Adjectives agree with their noun: add -e for feminine (grand → grande), -s for plural (grands, grandes).

Some change more: blanc → blanche, nouveau → nouvelle, gentil → gentille.

Most adjectives FOLLOW the noun (une maison blanche), but a small frequent set precedes it (grand, petit, bon, nouveau, joli).

points.title: Passé composé with avoir
points.function: Talk about completed past actions
points.explanation:
The everyday past = a present-tense form of avoir + the past participle: j'ai mangé 'I ate / have eaten'.

Regular participles: -er → -é (mangé), -ir → -i (fini), -re → -u (vendu).

The auxiliary is conjugated (ai, as, a, avons, avez, ont); the participle stays the same (no agreement with the subject when the auxiliary is avoir).

points.title: Passé composé with être
points.function: Use être for movement and reflexive verbs in the past
points.explanation:
A set of verbs of movement/change (aller, venir, partir, arriver, monter, descendre, naître, mourir, rester, tomber…) and all reflexive verbs form the past with être, not avoir: je suis allé 'I went'.

With être the participle AGREES with the subject in gender and number: elle est allée, ils sont partis, elles sont venues.

points.title: The imperfect (l'imparfait)
points.function: Describe ongoing or habitual past actions
points.explanation:
The imperfect describes a past that was ongoing, repeated, or a background state — English 'was …-ing' / 'used to'. Take the nous form of the present, drop -ons, add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient: mangeais 'I was eating', finissait 'he used to finish'. être is irregular (j'étais).

Contrast with the passé composé (one completed act).

points.title: The future (le futur simple)
points.function: Talk about what will happen
points.explanation:
The simple future adds -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont to the infinitive (dropping a final -e of -re verbs): je mangerai 'I will eat', il finira 'he will finish'.

Some stems are irregular: être → ser-, avoir → aur-, aller → ir-, faire → fer-, venir → viendr-.

points.title: Direct object pronouns (le, la, les…)
points.function: Replace the object with a short pronoun
points.explanation:
A known direct object becomes a pronoun placed before the verb: le (him/it m.), la (her/it f.), les (them), me, te, nous, vous.

Je le vois 'I see him', je les achète 'I'm buying them'. Before a vowel, me/te/le/la elide: je t'aime, je l'ai vu.

points.function: Replace 'to someone', a place, or a quantity

points.title: Comparative & superlative (plus… que, le plus)
points.function: Compare things
points.explanation:
The comparative uses plus / moins / aussi + adjective + que 'than/as': plus grand que 'bigger than', aussi cher que 'as expensive as'. The superlative adds the definite article: le plus grand 'the biggest'.

Irregular: bon → meilleur 'better', bien → mieux 'better (adv.)'.

points.title: Reflexive verbs (se laver)
points.function: Say the subject acts on itself
points.explanation:
Reflexive verbs carry a pronoun matching the subject: me, te, se, nous, vous, se, before the verb.

Je me lave 'I wash (myself)', il se lève 'he gets up', nous nous reposons 'we rest'. Many daily-routine verbs are reflexive.

points.title: Partitive articles (du, de la, des)
points.function: Say 'some' of an uncountable thing
points.explanation:
To talk about an unspecified quantity ('some'), French uses du (m.), de la (f.), de l' (before a vowel), des (pl.): je bois du café, je mange de la salade. After a negation, all become de/d': je ne bois pas de café.

After an expression of quantity too: beaucoup de café.

points.title: Possessive & demonstrative adjectives (mon, ce…)
points.function: Say 'my / this' and agree with the noun
points.explanation:
Possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner: mon/ma/mes 'my', ton/ta/tes 'your', son/sa/ses 'his/her', notre/nos, votre/vos, leur/leurs.

Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, use mon/ton/son (mon amie).

Demonstratives: ce/cet (m.), cette (f.), ces (pl.) 'this/these'.

points.title: The subjunctive (le subjonctif)
points.function: Express necessity, wish, emotion, and doubt
points.explanation:
After expressions of necessity, wish, emotion, or doubt — il faut que, je veux que, je suis content que, bien que — the verb goes into the subjunctive. For most verbs, take the ils form of the present, drop -ent, add -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent: que je parle, que nous finissions.

Key irregulars: être (sois), avoir (aie), faire (fasse), aller (aille).

points.title: The pluperfect (le plus-que-parfait)
points.function: Set one past action before another

The être/avoir and agreement rules are the same as the passé composé.

points.function: Recognize and use the formal written layer
points.explanation:
Formal/literary French keeps forms speech has dropped. The 'ne explétif' adds a meaningless ne after avant que, de peur que, and comparisons: je crains qu'il ne vienne 'I fear he will come'.

Elevated register also prefers connectors like néanmoins, toutefois, quoique, en dépit de, and the inverted question (viendrez-vous?).

references.title: Vitrine linguistique (BDL) — Office québécois de la langue française

drills.sentence: Je crains qu'il {{answer}} vienne trop tard.
drills.translation: I fear he will come too late. (ne explétif)
drills.hint: the semantically empty particle formal French slips in after a verb of fearing plus the subjunctive; it does not make the clause negative and takes no pas.

drills.sentence: Partez avant qu'il {{answer}} soit trop tard.
drills.translation: Leave before it's too late. (ne explétif)
drills.hint: the meaningless particle formal French adds inside a clause introduced by avant que; it negates nothing and pairs with no pas.

points.title: Key irregular presents (vais, fais, peux, veux)
points.function: Use the everyday irregular verbs
points.explanation:
The most useful French verbs bend the present tense:

aller (to go): vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont. faire (to do/make): fais, fait, faisons, faites, font. pouvoir (can): peux, peut, pouvons, peuvent. vouloir (to want): veux, veut, voulons, veulent. venir (to come): viens, vient, venons, viennent. prendre (to take): prends, prend, prenons, prennent.

Learn them on sight — they carry half of daily conversation, and aller/venir also build the near future and recent past.

related.title: Near future & recent past (aller / venir de)
related.contrast: The same vais/viens forms are the engines of je vais parler and je viens de parler.

points.title: The imperative (parle ! / ne parle pas !)
points.function: Tell or ask someone to do something
points.explanation:
The imperative uses the tu, nous, and vous present forms without the pronoun — and -er verbs drop the final -s in the tu form: Parle ! Allons-y ! Ouvrez la porte !

The negative wraps ne … pas around the verb: Ne parle pas. Pronouns follow an affirmative imperative with a hyphen (Donne-le-moi) but precede a negative one (Ne me le donne pas).

Irregulars worth knowing: sois/soyons/soyez (être), aie/ayons/ayez (avoir), va (aller — but vas-y !).

related.title: Negation with ne … pas
related.contrast: The same ne … pas frame wraps the imperative: Ne parle pas.

drills.translation: Speak more slowly, please.
drills.hint: tu command — -er verbs drop the final -s

drills.translation: Don't be late!
Open the door, please.
Let's go to the cinema together!

drills.sentence: Ne t'{{answer}} pas, on a encore le temps.
drills.translation: Don't worry, we still have time.
drills.hint: negative tu command of the reflexive verb meaning 'to worry' — its pronoun stands before the verb in the negative, and an -er tu command takes no final -s
